subChunks.title: Removing Rows — DELETE FROM
subChunks.hookHtml: DELETE is irreversible without a backup or transaction. The same rule as UPDATE: always include WHERE unless you genuinely want to empty the table.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Syntax

DELETE FROM apprentices WHERE id = 4;
DELETE FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0;

DELETE vs TRUNCATE

-- Slow but logged and reversible within a transaction:
DELETE FROM apprentices;

-- Fast, not individually logged, cannot be rolled back in most engines:
TRUNCATE TABLE apprentices;

TRUNCATE empties the table much faster by deallocating pages directly, but it bypasses row-level triggers and in many engines cannot be rolled back even inside a transaction.

Deleting with a subquery

-- Delete apprentices who have never completed a quest:
DELETE FROM apprentices
WHERE id NOT IN (
  SELECT DISTINCT apprentice_id FROM quest_completions
);

Soft delete pattern

Instead of actually deleting rows, many production systems add a deleted_at TIMESTAMP column and filter queries with WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. This preserves history and audit trails.

-- Soft delete:
UPDATE apprentices SET deleted_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE id = 4;
-- Query active only:
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

storyBeats.text: A Novice left the Academy yesterday, their record flagged for removal. Cipher pauses. 'Before we delete — are there completions attached to this apprentice?'

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: DELETE without WHERE empties the table. With foreign keys and CASCADE, deleting one row can cascade through several tables at once. Run the SELECT first. Consider whether soft delete — marking rows as deleted but keeping them — is better than hard delete for your use case.

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Using a subquery, delete all apprentices who have never completed any quest (their id does not appear in quest_completions). Write the SELECT version first, then the DELETE.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE, and describe the soft delete pattern and why it is often preferred in production.

questions.prompt: What does `DELETE FROM apprentices` (no WHERE) do?
options: Removes every row from the apprentices table
Throws an error — WHERE is required
questions.answer: Removes every row from the apprentices table
questions.explanation: DELETE without WHERE deletes all rows, leaving the table structure (columns, constraints, indexes) intact. The table still exists — it is now empty. TRUNCATE does the same thing much faster.

questions.prompt: A quest_completions table has ON DELETE CASCADE to apprentices. What happens when apprentice id=4 is deleted?
options: All quest_completion rows where apprentice_id=4 are automatically deleted too
The DELETE is rejected because completions exist
The apprentice row is deleted; completion rows retain their apprentice_id
The completions are set to NULL
questions.answer: All quest_completion rows where apprentice_id=4 are automatically deleted too
questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE propagates the delete to child rows. Deleting the parent (apprentice) triggers automatic deletion of all matching children (quest_completions).

questions.prompt: What is the soft delete pattern?
options: Marking rows as deleted (e.g. setting deleted_at = NOW()) instead of physically removing them
Using DELETE inside a transaction so it can be rolled back
Using a backup to reverse a delete
questions.answer: Marking rows as deleted (e.g. setting deleted_at = NOW()) instead of physically removing them
questions.explanation: Soft delete preserves data history and audit trails. Queries add WHERE deleted_at IS NULL to exclude soft-deleted rows. The original data is still recoverable and relationships remain intact.

questions.prompt: When would you choose TRUNCATE over DELETE for emptying a table?
options: When you need to remove all rows as fast as possible and do not need row-level logging or rollback
When you need to roll back the operation if something goes wrong
When triggers on the table must fire for each deleted row
When foreign key constraints reference the table
questions.answer: When you need to remove all rows as fast as possible and do not need row-level logging or rollback
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is much faster on large tables because it does not log individual row deletions. However: it typically cannot be rolled back, does not fire row-level triggers, and may not work if foreign keys reference the table (engine-specific).
